title: The Decline and Fall of Humboldt County

content_html_sanitized:
There’s an old saying in Texas, “You dance with the one what brung ya.” The grammar is a bit rough, but the meaning is clear, and it’s just good manners.

 

Unfortunately for Humboldt County, California forgot the debt that it owed to that beautiful part of the state when it legalized recreational cannabis in 2016 with the passage of Proposition 64, also known as the Adult Use of Marijuana Act.

 

Humboldt was the equivalent of “Champagne” and other “terroirs” that were perfect for growing the best of its kind.

 

There were also a large number of artisans who lived up in the foothills and were dedicated to growing the best of the best, which was then smuggled south on the Interstate where it brought premium prices.

 

Thanks to my old friend, Steve Tuck, I had the opportunity and/or excuse to visit several times.

See Steve Tuck Now Free and Getting Proper Medical Care. Will Return to Humboldt to Confront Medical Marijuana Cultivation Charges. The Many Issues In a Complex Case.

The natural beauty of Redwood country is still there, but the old economy was devastated by the attempt to industrialize cannabis production.

 

Unfortunately, the over regulation of cannabis production has not only perpetuated the black market, but it also destroyed the Humboldt artisanal cannabis culture.

 

Sadly, California Governor Gavin Newsom recently vetoed a bill to allow small marijuana growers to sell their products directly to consumers at state-organized farmers markets.

See California Governor Vetoes Bill To Let Marijuana Growers Sell  To Consumers At State-Run Farmers Markets

 

Consider that Northern California is also famous for its vineyards, some of which have tasting rooms where tourists can drink and buy bottles of the local wines to take home. Some of the vineyards even have inns with restaurants where wine connoisseurs can stay for dinner and spend a few days for an “immersive experience”.

 

Why can’t the cannabis world have the same thing?

 

In fairness to Governor Newsom, he did sign a bill allowing Cannabis cafes and entertainment zones, but where is the cannabis grown?

While Humboldt is a natural location for cannabis tourism, like wine tourism, there are many other areas that could also benefit from a new form of hospitality. However, encouraging local artisanal growing should be a part of killing the black market everywhere.

Given the size of the American cannabis market, there will always be a need for “Big Marijuana”, the boogeyman of the Big Prohibition, but there also needs to be a place for local growers to practice their craft. I have fond memories of visiting their gardens and enjoying their produce. Everyone should have the opportunity.
